title: State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. v. Dole (1986)
shortTitle: State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. v. Dole (1986)
summary: A challenge to a rule provision that will take effect only if a contingency occurs is not ripe when the contingency is unlikely and imposes no present hardship, while an agency's explained choice among restraint technologies survives arbitrary and capricious review.
notes:
Key line: "On such musings judicial review cannot properly be grounded." (Starr, J.)

Citation: 802 F.2d 474 (D.C. Cir. 1986).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company and the National Association of Independent Insurers, Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company, the American Insurance Association, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, two individuals, and the State of New York together with its Attorney General Robert Abrams, its Superintendent of Insurance and its Department of Insurance. The respondents were Elizabeth Dole, Secretary of Transportation, the Department of Transportation, Diane Steed, Administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, and the Administration. New Mexico, the Epilepsy Foundation, the American Academy of Pediatrics and others filed amicus briefs urging reversal.
sections.Material Facts: After the Supreme Court in 1983 held the rescission of the passive restraint standard arbitrary and capricious, the Department reopened rulemaking and on July 17, 1984, published a final rule amending Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208. The rule required phased installation of automatic occupant protection in new passenger cars, ten percent from September 1, 1986, rising to all cars after September 1, 1989, and allowed compliance by airbags, passive interiors, or detachable or nondetachable automatic belts. It also provided that the requirement would be rescinded if by April 1, 1989, states covering two thirds of the population enacted mandatory seat belt laws meeting specified conditions, including a $25 minimum penalty, with possible waivers for states whose laws predated August 1, 1984. By the time of decision twenty states covering about sixty percent of the population had passed belt laws, but none apparently complied with the conditions, and some states had drafted their laws to avoid counting.
sections.Procedural History: The insurers, the insurance commissioners and New York filed petitions for review of the final rule in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, which requires petitions within sixty days of promulgation. The consolidated cases, Nos. 84-1301 and 84-1459 through 84-1462, were argued on March 11, 1986, before Judges Mikva, Scalia and Starr. On September 18, 1986, the court, in an opinion by Judge Starr, dismissed all challenges to the rescission provision as unripe and denied New York's petition on the merits insofar as it challenged the Secretary's decision not to require airbags or nondetachable belts.
sections.Issue: Whether the petitioners' claims that the automatic rescission provision was arbitrary and capricious and contrary to the Safety Act, including New York's claim that the Secretary had no statutory power to try to influence state seat belt legislation, were ripe for judicial review under Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner when the rescission might never occur. And whether the Secretary acted arbitrarily and capriciously by allowing compliance through detachable automatic belts, by declining to require airbags in all cars, and by allegedly failing to consider requiring both airbags and nondetachable belts.
sections.Holding: The court held the attacks on the rescission provision unripe. Although the rule was final and the questions largely legal, the record showed that rescission was singularly unlikely, so a decision might prove unnecessary, and the petitioners' asserted hardships, future deaths, dampened technological development, and weakened state lobbying efforts, were either speculative, not their own, or mere planning uncertainty. New York's challenge to the choice of technologies was ripe because installation was to begin on September 1, 1986. On the merits the court held that the Secretary had adequately explained her refusal to exclude detachable belts, to mandate airbags, or to require airbags plus nondetachable belts, so the rule was not arbitrary and capricious.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Starr applied the two part Abbott Laboratories test, fitness of the issues and hardship from withholding review. On fitness, the institutional interest in avoiding speculative controversies was powerful because the trap door would likely never open, and if rescission ever appeared imminent the petitioners could seek review and a stay then. On hardship, deaths would occur only if rescission occurred; claims that automakers would delay development asked the court to gaze into a crystal ball; and the states whose dilemmas were invoked were not before the court, could insert sunset clauses in their laws, and faced nothing like the coerced primary conduct in Abbott Laboratories. Uncertainty in lobbying strategy was like the planning uncertainty rejected in Tennessee Gas Pipeline. New York's statutory coercion claim was unripe because New York had no pending legislation on which any coercion was operating. On the merits, State Farm required only a rational connection between facts and choice. The Secretary rejected a nondetachable belt requirement because surveys showed ten to twenty percent of the public would cut such belts and because they would force elimination of the center front seat; she rejected an airbag mandate because airbags cost an estimated $320 more per car and $800 to replace and because of public acceptance concerns, considerations the Supreme Court had said she could weigh; and a rule section titled Airbags and/or Non-Detachable Seatbelts showed she had considered the combination.

topics.lrs-n-hard-look: The remand litigation sustained technological choices after the agency considered their costs, safety effects, and public acceptance.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Mikva concurred in part and dissented in part. He agreed that most challenges to the rescission provision were unripe but would have treated New York's claim that the Secretary failed to consider combining a passive restraint requirement with mandatory use laws as ripe, and he found all four of New York's claims meritorious: the record suggested that restraints plus belt laws would save more lives than either alone, the incentive scheme reached driver behavior that the Safety Act left to the states, the evidence favored nondetachable belts, the airbag cost rationale was almost silly given that few airbags deploy inadvertently, and the rule was silent on airbags combined with nondetachable belts.
